The story develops its characters to the exact level of complexity their roles require. Daniel is a fully realized complex character who undergoes internal growth, learning to confront and release the lingering, unexamined remnants of his past marriage. Crucially, his partner Isabel is not treated merely as a flat plot device to help him solve his problem; the author gives her a distinct personality (such as intentionally cooking fish badly to prompt a serious conversation), her own parallel backstory with her ex-partner Gareth, and her own moment of emotional evolution when she finally deletes Gareth's voicemail. Meanwhile, peripheral figures who only exist in memory—such as Rachel, Gareth, and Mrs. Okafor—are appropriately kept as flat characters, given just enough specific detail to feel real and serve the themes of the story without unnecessarily cluttering the narrative.
